To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

protonation of histidines in the S5–S6 linker of Kv1.5 accelerates inactivation and decreases peak current amplitude and that this effect is mediated by a group of residues that includes histidine 463 and the adjacent turret region.
protonation of H463 in the Kv1. 5 turret increases the rate of P/C-type inactiva- tion and decreases the peak amplitude of the current.
the side chain of histidine 462, which is located at the distal end of the S5-P region, can modulate slow inactivation in a manner similar to that of histidine 464.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of inactivation in voltage-gated K(+) channels.
the role of the turret region of the S5-P helix linker in the inactivation process in voltage-gated potassium channels.
the modulation of slow inactivation in potassium channels by the pore turret and its implications for the mechanism of slow inactivation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
protonation of H463 in Kv1.4 is not a direct mechanism for modulating inactivation.
protonation of histidines in the turret region can accelerate slow inactivation in voltage-gated K+ channels.
SCAM analysis reveals that a discrete region of turret (E456-P462) is involved in slow inactivation of Kv1.5 and this region is modulated by protonation of H463 in the S4-P linker.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pore turret region of Kv1.5 plays a critical role in modulating P/C-type inactivaiton and that residue 464 is the most sensitive residue within the turret region to protonation.
the turret region is a discrete, functionally significant region of the channel that can modulate slow inactivation.

protonation of H463 in the turret of Kv1.5 increases the rate of inactivation and decreases current amplitude by altering the local environment of the turret and/or by altering the interaction of the turret with the S4 segment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the turret is a region of the channel that is critical for slow inactivation and that this region is highly conserved among the Kv1 subfamily of channels.
the turret region of the voltage-sensing domain is a dynamic region of the protein that can be manipulated to alter the macroscopic current.
the turret region is an important modulator of P/C-type inactivity.
